tables.note: Persistence is the diagonal of the transition matrix: the probability of still being in that regime tomorrow.

notes: Regimes are estimated on the broad market (Mkt-RF) over 9,212 observations, not on the portfolio: a regime is a property of the environment, which the portfolio then inherits. States are canonicalised by ascending volatility, so labels stay stable across refits.
Charts are restricted to the portfolio window from 2018-01-01; the parameter table above reflects the full fitted history.

Beta is cov(p,m)/var(m). In stress both the covariance and the market variance inflate and can largely cancel, so beta may stay flat or even fall while absolute risk rises sharply. Volatility is the robust effect; beta and correlation are conditional.

sections.title: Stress testing
sections.subtitle: Historical replays and parametric shocks through the factor betas

rows.description: Global Financial Crisis: Lehman collapse to market trough
Euro sovereign debt crisis / US downgrade selloff
Taper tantrum: rates spike on Fed tapering signal
Q4 2018 selloff: rate-hike fears, growth scare
COVID-19 crash: fastest bear market on record
2022 inflation shock: aggressive Fed hikes, stocks and bonds down together
Sharp rotation into value, mild market decline
Flight to quality during a market drop

notes: Historical scenarios are replayed by applying the portfolio's current factor betas to the factor returns of that window, so they work for crises that predate the ETFs themselves. They capture the systematic PnL only.

These figures likely UNDERSTATE the true loss: the betas are full-sample and held constant, while in real crises betas and correlations typically rise. The rolling-beta chart on the factor page shows how much that assumption is violated.

stats.hint: Σ|w| — leverage the unconstrained solution takes on

figures.title: Efficient frontier
figures.note: Expected returns are historical means, used here only to give the frontier a vertical axis — see the caveat below.

notes: Minimum variance needs no expected returns, which is exactly what makes it robust: μ is the noisiest input in mean-variance and the one that drives error maximisation. The long-only constraint acts as an implicit regulariser (Jagannathan & Ma 2003).
The frontier does need μ, and here it is the historical mean — a poor forecast, shown for construction purposes only. In practice μ would come from Black-Litterman or explicit views.
The long-short solution reaches 10.11% volatility but with 1.45× gross exposure: large offsetting legs fitted to the noise in Σ.
